UTSA DATATHON / WORKING PROTOTYPE

Where could we capture stormwater?

A San Antonio terrain-screening pilot with real USGS elevation and city drainage data, historical Texas image evidence, and a transparent collector-storage experiment.

Current result: investigation points, not optimal construction sites. Rainfall below is a user-defined scenario. AI image analysis uses the supplied API; Earth-2 is not used. This model does not predict flood depth, damage, homes protected, tunnel performance, or construction suitability.

1. Follow the terrain

West-side pilot bounding box: −98.57 to −98.50 longitude, 29.39 to 29.46 latitude. Points rank by upstream area within the cropped raster, with slopes below 8° and a 350 m minimum separation. Current pipes and channels are context overlays; their hydraulic operation is not modeled.

UTM zone 14N, approximately 17.1 × 17.3 metres per cell. This is a cropped pilot, not a full watershed: external inflows are omitted. Sink filling and a single-flow drainage tree simplify urban surface flow. No parcel, building, utility-conflict, soil, habitat, or ownership screening has been applied.

2. Compare collector storage assumptions

Event runoff volume = rainfall × area × runoff coefficient. All eight candidate collectors receive the same assumed storage capacity. Collectors fill once, and downstream collectors receive only water not already captured. Capture is an optimistic volume bound because inlet rates are unlimited.

Generated runoff
Captured volume
Capture fraction

These are scenario assumptions, not observed rainfall or Earth-2 predictions. Stored water must eventually be drained or reused; this model does not estimate peak-flow reduction.

4. Keep imagery evidence geographically honest

The provided metadata contains 1,204 Texas aerial images and 273 fields. None lie within our broad San Antonio bounding box. Human flood labels are blank. Six images (three before/after pairs) are cached for demonstration; all metadata is retained. Image review supports evidence gathering, not calibrated flood-depth estimation. Differences in season, year, and imaging affect comparisons.

Live AI evidence review

Three image pairs were analyzed through the supplied OpenAI-compatible API. The responses below are actual cached model outputs, not examples. They describe Houston imagery and do not determine the San Antonio site ranking.

TX001 — Bear Creek / west Houston

qwen3-vl-8b-instruct | 2026-11-13T19:15:27.632588+00:00

Image B shows widespread water covering streets and yards, submerging roads and surrounding vegetation. In Image A, these areas are dry. One important uncertainty: it is unclear whether the water in Image B is from a natural flood or a man-made source like a canal or reservoir. The water appears to be flowing through residential areas, but its origin and cause cannot be determined from the images alone.

TX002 — Bear Creek / west Houston

qwen3-vl-8b-instruct | 2026-11-13T19:15:29.425692+00:00

Image B shows widespread brown water covering streets and yards, submerging roads and surrounding vegetation. In Image A, these areas are dry. The water in Image B appears to have inundated multiple residential blocks, obscuring driveways and sidewalks. Uncertainty: It is unclear whether the water is from a single event or multiple events, and whether the water level is rising or receding. The images do not show water depth, damage, or the number of homes affected. The water is not confined to channels; it spreads across residential lots and streets. The images show the Houston area, not San Antonio.

TX003 — Bear Creek / west Houston

qwen3-vl-8b-instruct | 2026-11-13T19:15:31.662081+00:00

Image B shows extensive muddy water covering areas not visible in Image A, including regions where vegetation and a road were previously exposed. The water appears to have inundated the forest floor and partially submerged the road, which is now obscured by sediment. Uncertainty: It is unclear whether the water is from a natural stream overflow or a flood event, as no man-made structures or clear water channels are visible to confirm a flood source or extent. The images do not show buildings or infrastructure to assess impact.

AI observations have not been human-validated. Source images, prompts, timestamps, model IDs and image hashes are retained in results/api_evidence. No API credential is embedded in this report.

5. Construction: next validation steps

The completed demonstration uses a laptop, the supplied Qwen vision API, and scenario rainfall. Earth-2 is not part of the active workflow. The optional forecast runner is retained only for future development; no weather forecast is claimed.

For tunnel and new-construction comparisons, assemble pipe topology, invert elevations, capacities, outfalls and downstream boundary conditions; buildings and parcels; soils and protected areas; and a complete watershed DEM. Calibrate an EPA SWMM or coupled surface-flow model before optimizing cost and residential exposure reduction. New construction also adds runoff and must be evaluated for downstream impacts.
